title: Two-Layer Grid-Following/Grid-Forming Operating-Mode Configuration for Photovoltaic–Battery Energy Storage Plants Considering Operating Power and Branch Impedance
abstract: As photovoltaic penetration increases, dynamic interactions among inverters pose growing stability challenges for renewable energy plants connected to weak grids. In hybrid power plants comprising photovoltaic (PV) generation and battery energy storage systems (BESSs), hereafter referred to as PV-BESS plants, operating selected BESS inverters in grid-forming (GFM) mode can improve stability under weak-grid conditions. However, when BESS units differ in operating power and branch impedance, allocations with the same number of GFM units can exhibit different stability boundaries. Mode configuration must therefore specify both the number of GFM units and which units operate in this mode. To address this issue, this paper proposes a two-layer operating-mode configuration method that incorporates unit-specific operating power and branch impedance. The method is built on a plant-level dq-domain impedance model that represents each inverter’s control mode, steady-state operating point, and branch impedance. In the first layer, a homogeneous reduced-order model is used to determine a candidate GFM unit number. In the second layer, the actual operating power and branch impedance of each unit are restored; the steady-state feasibility and small-signal stability of different mode allocations are jointly evaluated; and the feasible allocation with the largest relative short-circuit-ratio margin is selected. Theoretical analysis shows that the number of GFM units influences the plant’s aggregate grid-forming support. Differences in operating power and branch impedance result in allocation-dependent critical SCRs and stability margins, even when the GFM unit count is fixed. MATLAB/Simulink simulations support the choice of the candidate GFM unit count and confirm the predicted stability differences among mode allocations.
title_zh: Two-Layer Grid-Following/Grid-Forming Operating-Mode Configuration for Photovoltaic–Battery Energy Storage Plants Considering Operating Power and Branch Impedance

title: EDGE AI-BASED REAL-TIME BATTERY MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS: TECHNOLOGY TRENDS AND DESIGN FRAMEWORK
abstract: Battery management systems (BMSs) increasingly require low-latency, reliable, and intelligent processing capabilities to support the rapid expansion of electric vehicles and stationary energy storage systems. Conventional centralized and cloud-dependent BMS architectures can provide advanced analytics but may face limitations associated with communication latency, network dependence, data transmission overhead, and privacy. Edge artificial intelligence (Edge AI) provides an alternative approach by performing data processing and intelligent inference close to the battery system. This review examines major technology trends in real-time BMSs and proposes a reference design framework for Edge AI-based battery management. Recent developments in battery sensing, artificial intelligence-based state estimation, decentralized computing, lightweight machine learning, digital twins, communication, and cybersecurity are reviewed. Based on these trends, a layered framework is proposed in which battery sensors and embedded controllers acquire operating data, edge processors perform preprocessing and intelligent analysis, and cloud platforms provide long-term data management, model updating, and fleet-level analytics. The framework emphasizes local state estimation, anomaly detection, predictive maintenance, secure edge-cloud communication, and optional digital-twin integration. The review indicates that Edge AI can reduce dependence on continuous cloud connectivity and enable faster decision-making, although practical deployment remains constrained by limited embedded resources, model complexity, cybersecurity risks, heterogeneous battery platforms, and interoperability issues. Future BMS development is expected to combine lightweight AI, adaptive edge-cloud collaboration, explainable decision support, digital twins, and security-by-design principles.
venue: International Journal of Science and Research Archive

title: Multi-Task SOC/SOH Estimation and Cross-Domain SOC Transfer for Sodium-Ion Batteries: From Cells to Battery Packs
abstract: Sodium-ion batteries are promising for cost-sensitive and low-temperature electric-vehicle applications, yet reliable battery management systems (BMSs) require evaluation beyond a development cell. This study develops a lightweight multi-task gated recurrent unit (GRU) framework that integrates timestep-level state-of-charge (SOC) estimation with window-based, cycle-informed state-of-health (SOH) estimation. The main A6 configuration uses aging-sensitive descriptors and contains 24,882 trainable parameters. On the NFM source-domain test set, A6 achieves 1.078% SOC root-mean-square error (RMSE), 0.978% cycle-aggregated SOH RMSE, and an SOH coefficient of determination (R2) of 0.835, compared with 2.409% SOH RMSE for the constant-mean baseline. An ablation analysis distinguishes the effects of task coupling and input observability. A separate three-input source-trained backbone is evaluated for external SOC transfer: on Hina, zero-shot RMSE is 22.5–36.2%, and calibration with 25% of the target cell’s 25 °C records reduces errors at unseen temperatures to 14.0–27.4%; on the CVUT 4S11P cold-start battery pack, zero-shot RMSE of approximately 27–29% decreases to 12.0–19.7% following adaptation on the first 25% of time-ordered records. The separate source-domain and transfer tests show why low in-domain error alone cannot establish SOC accuracy on a different commercial cell or battery pack, even when limited target-domain calibration is available.
title_zh: Multi-Task SOC/SOH Estimation and Cross-Domain SOC Transfer for Sodium-Ion Batteries: From Cells to Battery Packs
